Makrothumia
ma-kroh-thoo-MEE-ah
n. (Greek)
Greek makrothumia, literally long-tempered-ness, from makros (long) + thumos (passion, temper). The fundamental sense is the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger, which becomes by extension patience, longsuffering, endurance with persons.

📖 Biblical Definition

Makrothumia is one of the great virtue-nouns of the New Testament, and the KJV renders it consistently as longsuffering—a coined English compound that captures the Greek’s sense better than the colorless modern patience. The word is built from makros (long) and thumos (passion, temper); its literal sense is long-tempered, the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger that gives space and time for the offender to repent and be restored. The supreme exemplar is God Himself. He is named longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin (Ex 34:6-7—the LXX uses makrothumos); Paul says the riches of God’s longsuffering and goodness leadeth thee to repentance (Rom 2:4); Peter explains the apparent delay of Christ’s return as the Lord is not slack concerning his promise... but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance (2 Pet 3:9). God’s longsuffering is the deliberate withholding of deserved judgment to make space for repentance; the patience-shaped mercy by which the wrath is restrained while the gospel is offered. The same virtue is to characterize the saints. Makrothumia is the fourth fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22 (love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance). It is commanded as a mark of Christian community: with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love (Eph 4:2); put on therefore... bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering (Col 3:12). It is required of ministers especially: preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine (2 Tim 4:2). The category is therefore the patient bearing-with-persons (as distinct from hupomonē, the patient bearing-with-circumstances): the deliberate, willed, sustained patience with the brother who is slow to grow, the spouse who is slow to change, the child who is slow to mature, the unbeliever who is slow to repent, the saint who has wronged us and not yet seen it. The KJV’s longsuffering is therefore a brilliant rendering: it captures the temporal-extension (long) and the suffering-with-persons (suffering) that the Greek compound names, and produces an English term that has shaped the church’s understanding of the virtue for four centuries.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LONGSUFFERING as bearing injuries or provocations for a long time; patient; not easily provoked; in scripture, the Spirit-wrought patience with persons that is the fruit of the Spirit, modeled supremely on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners.

expand to see more

LONGSUFFERING, a. — Bearing injuries or provocations for a long time; patient; not easily provoked. The Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish (2 Pet 3:9).

MAKROTHUMIA — (Greek term.) Long-tempered-ness; the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger; patience with persons; longsuffering. Listed as the fourth fruit of the Spirit in Gal 5:22.

📖 Key Scripture

Galatians 5:22 — "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith..."

Romans 2:4 — "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?"

2 Peter 3:9 — "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Colossians 3:12 — "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Makrothumia is corrupted, on one side, by the impatience register of late-modern culture that has trained the believer to react quickly, sever relationships at the first friction, and lose the long-temper that is the Spirit-wrought patience with persons—and on the other by the despairing-presumption that mistakes God’s longsuffering for indifference and proceeds in sin as though no day of judgment will come.

expand to see more

The impatience register of late-modern culture has trained the believer out of makrothumia. The cultural patterns are uniform: immediate gratification, rapid response, severance of relationships at the first significant friction, intolerance of slow growth in others, refusal to extend the long patience with persons that the gospel commands. The believer who absorbs these patterns brings them to the church and the family: brothers are cut off for offenses that longsuffering would have absorbed, marriages are abandoned where longsuffering would have borne with the slow growth of a beloved spouse, parents grow impatient with the slow maturing of children, churches fragment over personality frictions that longsuffering would have softened. The recovery is the Spirit’s work, not human grit: makrothumia is the fruit of the Spirit, given as the Spirit fills and sanctifies the saint over time. The discipline is to ask for it, cultivate it through deliberate practice (especially with the persons whose presence most provokes its opposite), and to repent of every reactive impatience that has substituted for the long-tempered patience God Himself models.

The opposite corruption is the despairing-presumption that mistakes God’s longsuffering for indifference. Peter explicitly addresses it: the Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. The very delay of Christ’s return that the scoffers cite as evidence God will not judge is in fact evidence of His longsuffering, deliberately extending the day of grace to give space for repentance. The presumption of those who therefore presume their sin will be tolerated forever, that the day of judgment has been canceled, that God’s patience proves His indifference, is precisely the misreading Peter refutes. Recover both ends. Refuse the impatience that has lost makrothumia as a saint’s virtue, and refuse the presumption that misreads God’s makrothumia as indifference. The biblical pattern is the saint who has received God’s longsuffering with thanksgiving, extends the same to others as the fruit the Spirit produces, and lives in sober expectation of the day when the longsuffering interval will close and the just Judge will come.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek makrothumia (long-tempered-ness, longsuffering, patience with persons), from makros (long) + thumos (passion, temper); the Spirit-wrought patience with persons (distinct from hupomonē, patience with circumstances), modeled supremely on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners.

expand to see more

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience with persons (Gal 5:22; Eph 4:2; Col 1:11; 3:12; 1 Tim 1:16; 2 Tim 3:10; 4:2; Heb 6:12; Jas 5:10; 1 Pet 3:20; 2 Pet 3:9, 15).

Greek makrothumeō (G3114) — to be longsuffering (Matt 18:26, 29; Luke 18:7; 1 Cor 13:4; 1 Thess 5:14; Heb 6:15; Jas 5:7-8; 2 Pet 3:9).

Greek makrothumos (G3116) — longsuffering (the adjective; LXX of Ex 34:6 of God).

Greek hupomonē (G5281) — patience with circumstances, endurance (the cousin virtue).

Usage

"The Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish—God’s longsuffering deliberately extends the day of grace."

"Makrothumia is the patience with persons, distinct from hupomonē, the patience with circumstances; the saint needs both."

"Impatience culture loses the virtue; despairing-presumption misreads God’s longsuffering as indifference; biblical pattern is Spirit-wrought patience with persons modeled on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners."
